title: The Safavids
hookLine: a Sufi family from Ardabil takes a throne, and Twelver Shi'ism becomes the faith of Iran

cards: In Mashhad, in the northeast of Iran, a golden dome rises over a grave. Day and night, people come: pilgrims off long bus rides, students, grandmothers, families with small children asleep on their shoulders.
They touch the lattice around the tomb, pray, weep, sit on the courtyard carpets and talk. The man buried there is Imam Reza, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
For Shi'a Muslims he is one of the Imams, the rightful guides of the community. Iran had not always been a Shi'a land. Today, the family that made it one.

teach.b: The Safavids began not as kings but as a Sufi order, led by a family of sheikhs in the town of Ardabil, in the northwest of Iran.
Their followers were devoted, Turkish-speaking horsemen among them who wore a red cap and were called the Qizilbash, the red heads.

Out of that order came a young leader named Isma'il, who took the old Persian title of shah and won a kingdom. And he made one choice that shaped Iran: Twelver Shi'ism would be the faith of the state.

Twelver Shi'a Muslims hold that leadership after the Prophet belonged to his family, beginning with his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and passing through a line of Imams, the last of whom is in hiding and will return.
Sunni Muslims hold that the community rightly chose its leaders, the caliphs. Both read the same Qur'an. One verse shows how a single line can be heard two ways.

The Prophet is told to say that he asks no payment for his message, only love for those near of kin. Shi'a commentators hear the Prophet's family in it; Sunni commentators have also read it in other ways.
The Safavid change was not gentle everywhere. Scholars were brought in, Sunni practice was pushed out, and Iran grew apart from its Ottoman neighbors, who were Sunni and often at war with the shahs.
The shrines grew in honor: Imam Reza in Mashhad, his sister Fatima Masuma in Qom. A whole country's map of pilgrimage was redrawn.

how: Shi'a Muslims in Iran and beyond make pilgrimage to the shrines of the Imams and their families, such as Imam Reza in Mashhad and Fatima Masuma in Qom, to pray, read and remember them.

games.q: you're Isma'il, the young leader of a Sufi order, and you've just won a kingdom. your neighbors to the west are Sunni Ottomans. what faith do you make the faith of your state?
o: whatever most of your new subjects already follow.
Twelver Shi'ism, the faith of your order.
none at all: the state stays out of it.
games.why: he made Twelver Shi'ism the faith of the state, brought in scholars, and pushed out Sunni practice. Iran grew apart from its Ottoman neighbors.

practice: Bring back the courtyard in Mashhad: the carpets, the families, the gold dome.

Then think of a place where people you love are buried, or a place you return to when you need to remember who you belong to, and what people bring there. If you pray, you can pray for those who travel to such places.

wordCard.voice: The Safavids. A Sufi family from Ardabil that became shahs of Iran and made Twelver Shi'ism the faith of the state. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: Safavi, a name usually traced to Sheikh Safi al-Din of Ardabil, whose Sufi order the family led.

carryVoice: Your line: iran becomes shia. It closes a week of empires: the Ottomans rising, Istanbul, Hagia Sophia, the lawgiver, the architect, the millet, and now the shahs. See you tomorrow.
